prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Having read all eight ballots, I move topological insulators to the top of my own list. Seven of eight members ranked B039, which is the broadest support on the shortlist, and the support comes from members with different backgrounds. That is more informative than first-place counts alone. Scientifically it is a clean theory-then-experiment story: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall idea, and Molenkamp's group saw the quantised edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells. It then spread through many materials and many laboratories, including ARPES on three-dimensional Bi-based insulators, over roughly fifteen to twenty years. Band topology is a new organising principle and not just a tool. The 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type phases of Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz, but not time-reversal-invariant topological insulators. I know this field as a neighbour of mesoscopic superconductivity, edge states and Majorana physics, and I defer to Eriksson and Mehlig on the finer condensed-matter points. A prize here would be mature rather than premature.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weak point. The supplied credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal Molenkamp's experiment tested directly, and Zhang has died. It also leaves out Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy for the three-dimensional case, and Hasan and Cava for its experimental discovery. A three-person limit forces a contestable split, and a prize that rests on one reading of the priority history is less robust than one where the credit is obvious, as it is for optical lattice clocks. I am also working outside my core field, so my confidence in the priority history is lower than for the AMO and superconducting-circuit candidates.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a theory-experiment loop that gave electronic-structure theory a language for classifying materials, while admitting the trio is defensible but not uncontested and that he relies on memory for the priority history.
responses.response: I agree on the importance and on the loop. The edge-transport measurement closes it in a way a purely theoretical classification would not. I would go further on the weakness. The decisive HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction and not the original Kane-Mele graphene proposal, because spin-orbit coupling in graphene is far too small. The citation therefore has to name the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant carefully, so that Molenkamp's credit is for the realisation and not for a prediction he did not make. Your point on first-principles classification of materials by topological invariants is a strong maturity argument, and I accept it. Whether it is enough to settle the BHZ omission I leave to the committee.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first, calling it precision atomic physics at its best with an easily localised credit. She ranks circuit QED only seventh because the 2025 prize recognised superconducting-circuit quantum effects, so an adjacent award would be debatable.
responses.response: Your timing objection to circuit QED is fair. I am the person on this committee who ranked it first, so I should say it clearly: 2025 honoured macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in circuits, and circuit QED is a different discovery. It is strong-coupling light-matter physics at the single-photon level. But I accept that two superconducting-circuit prizes in consecutive years would be hard to defend, and my own ties to this community are another reason to lower it. On clocks, I largely agree with you on the science and on the clean Katori-Ye attribution. My reservation is that the practical culmination, the redefinition of the second, is still pending. That does not weigh against the discovery, but it is why I put it second behind a broader and more clearly overdue field.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a measurement technique that moves the limit of what can be observed, with independent confirmation at several national laboratories and applications in fundamental-constant tests, geodesy and dark-matter searches.
responses.response: I take your argument seriously. A technique that several laboratories reproduce at the 10^-18 level is about as robust as experimental physics gets, and the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. I would not oppose B022 and have listed it as my first alternative. Where I differ is on how much weight the instrument-first criterion should carry against a new class of matter. The lattice clock makes existing physics more precisely measurable, while topological insulators changed what condensed-matter physicists look for. I also expect the pending SI redefinition to make the clock case stronger in a year or two, while the topological insulator case is already complete.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first as an overdue experimental closure of the Standard Model, but concedes that three-person credit for a collaboration of thousands is a real allocation problem.
responses.response: The physics case is certainly exceptional, and I defer to you and Pearce on particle physics. My concern is exactly the one you raise: it is a project-leadership award, and I am not sure it reflects who made the decisive individual contributions. Pearce called such an award at odds with the committee's emphasis on specific contributions. Without a resolution of that tension I cannot put B028 above candidates with a clearer individual-credit structure. If you can show how the leadership credit would withstand scrutiny, I would want to hear it.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first because band topology gives robust boundary states across condensed matter, materials and cold atoms, and he notes the fairness question over the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and three-dimensional-case names missing from the credit.
responses.response: I agree on the generality. The cold-atom connection is a good point, since topological bands are now engineered in optical lattices and in circuit platforms, which shows the concept is not tied to one material. On fairness, I think we should not decide on grounds of tidiness. If the committee believes the prize is only defensible with Bernevig and Hughes, it should say so and not cut a trio that hides the problem. Within the supplied names, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the most coherent set.

uncertainties: Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes (and the late Zhang) and of the three-dimensional-insulator contributors makes the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio unfair or whether it is a reasonable reading of priority.
Whether two superconducting-circuit prizes in consecutive years (2025 and circuit QED now) are acceptable. I now lean no, but I am not the right person to decide that.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should make the committee wait for the optical-lattice-clock prize or whether the physics is already complete.
Whether any two-part combination would stay within three people. The two strongest candidates, B039 and B022, total five credited names, so a shared prize would need a subset of one.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT at Chalmers and work in superconducting circuits. I was a co-author on the dynamical Casimir effect experiment and have close ties to groups around circuit QED (as a theorist in the same community I know the B023 candidates professionally, and Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson are my Chalmers colleagues). That is a specific connection that may require recusal on B023, and I have therefore moved it to an alternative and not the preferred configuration. Chalmers has hosted Clarke and Martinis, 2025 laureates. No specific connection to B039, B022, B005 or B025 is apparent from the provided profile.
